Git code and code history
If we identified that the idx_c4333a3a problem is caused by bad code, it's time to find out who wrote that
code originally or whether this code was recently changed. Looking at Git commit history is
the right place to start. An MCP server can easily analyze commit history to identify all relevant
code changes to a particular file, class, or function. When the code agent suggests code changes
to fix the problem, the agent can include the change history to ensure that things that were
fixed with a previous code commit don't break again. It also allows an agent to open up a Slack
channel with all involved developers who made code changes recently, present the evidence,
and ask for collaboration to find a solution.
Automating all idx_d3a71957 of this through an AI agent optimizes the otherwise manual tasks for a single
person to do the research manually and come up with similar conclusions.
Software catalog
Before making any idx_5052e4fe changes, it's good to know the potential impact on upstream or
downstream dependencies. If a fix includes calls to a new downstream service, then this
service will see an increase in traffic, and they must be prepared for it. If a fix includes changing
the behavior of our response, for example, changing performance behavior or a change in
service response body, then the upstream services that call us need to be informed.
Service catalogs are a good way to keep track of dependencies. They can either be managed
through idx_1e89f1d9 an internal development platform (IDP) such as Backstage, Port, Cortex, or Kratix.
Service catalogs can also be found in Configuration Management Databases (CMDBs) in
tools idx_06383f0c such as ServiceNow or BMC. Modern observability tools can also be a good source of
service catalog, assuming that you have enriched logs, metrics, and traces with metadata,
which we discussed in Chapter 3 in the Context is king section. Whatever your source is,
connecting that source through an MCP with the agentic AI allows that agent to make risk
assessments on changing the behavior through a code change. This will be additional
information presented to the engineers to make a faster, more informed decision about how to
fix the problem at hand.
As you can see, there are many tools that can be involved in an agentic AI workflow when an
engineer prompts it with the following: Analyze the current problems identified for the services I am
responsible for. Assess which problems to fix first and why. Identify the root cause, propose fixes where
necessary, and provide a risk assessment for deploying the changes.
By now, you have a good understanding of the power of agentic AI as it leverages observability
data, code insights, or ticket information through local or remote MCP servers.

Chapter 6 204
The recap on agentic AI and MCP has refreshed our memories on those important components
so that we can idx_3f7b4968 continue discussing how to best connect your observability data with the
agentic AI to maximize its impact.
Connecting observability data to your agentic AI
When prompting Tell me which problems I have in the services I am responsible for, the question is
how does the AI agent idx_83055ffe know which data it can query from idx_efd5f0e6 the observability platform to answer
this question? What is a problem anyway? Would we see this in logs or metrics? Or is there a
concept of a problem in the observability platform? How can we make sure that an agent is not
executing queries that are not efficient, resulting in high licensing costs? How can we make
sure the agent cannot access any confidential data or data not relevant to the task it's working
on? How can we make sure no confidential observability data gets exposed to other systems
that the agent talks to as well?
These are all very good and important questions to answer before moving on with a large-scale
implementation and rollout of your observability agent implementation. In this section, we
therefore focus on how to connect your observability platform, how to track usage, and how to
train the agent to become acquainted with observability to become more efficient when
executing tasks.
In this chapter, we treat our observability agent as an apprentice that we help to become a
master in observability. As in any trade, becoming a master starts with being trained on how to
use specific tools, for example, a hammer, a saw, and a screwdriver. This is followed by clear
guidance and feedback on how to become efficient with those tools and use them in
combination in order to achieve a certain goal, for example, crafting a table. We also
continuously measure the usage of tools and the outcomes to see when and whether our
apprentice reaches mastery.
As we raised the security and compliance aspect, Chapter 9 provides a more detailed
explanation of how to secure your AI and fine-tune your AI. If that's a topic of interest, look
into the sections titled Building trust in the AI and Securing the AI.
Now, back to our observability agent. We start with an apprentice that initially only
understands our written words, thanks to LLMs, but doesn't really know what to do with our
requests. We then define the tools, which are how we can access certain observability data
through an observability MCP server, for example, list current problems, and return critical log
messages. After that, we idx_b16acead provide guidance through instruction idx_50f70040 files on how to achieve a bigger
task, for example, list all the active problems and find the relevant critical logs for them. We
measure the results, refine the instructions, and give feedback on the results achieved until we

have our master observability agent.
205 The Observability Agent: Real-Life Use Cases
Defining tools: Connecting your observability platform
through MCP
There is no need to idx_0b4141c2 go into the technical details on how to build an MCP server, as there is a lot
of documentation available online that you can follow [4]. Chances are that your observability
platform already provides an MCP server that you can either run locally or leverage as a
remotely hosted version. Many enterprises we have seen often start with the available MCP,
but sometimes decide to build their own to better control the available tools for the agents.
Another reason is to provide an MCP server with a set of tools independent of the backend
observability platform. So, when the platform in the back changes, or if there is more than one
platform used, then the MCP server acts like a transparent proxy.
Whether you build an MCP server from scratch or modify one for your own needs, there are
some considerations for the architecture and definition of the exported tools. Kudos to
Christian K., senior software engineer, who shared a lot of his learnings when building the first
open source MCP server for Dynatrace.
Start with the questions you need to answer
Put yourself in the shoes of the engineers who use an AI agent. What will they prompt, what
would an observability expert do to get the answer, and how would we make that information
queryable through the MCP? Christian's first use case was " I want to know which problems I have
in my application." The observability expert would have opened the observability tool and
looked at the currently opened alerts that the tool detected. As the terminology of his
observability uses problems instead of alerts, he decided to call the first tool of his MCP server
list_problems. That tool basically queried the API of the observability tool to return the
current list of open alerts. A short time after, other developers came to him and said that their
prompt would be Show me problems from yesterday, which required a change in the
list_problems tool to also include a timeframe parameter.
Whether it is about querying problems, incidents, alerts, metrics, logs, traces, events, synthetic
test results, SLOs, error budgets, or topology data, start by understanding the questions that
will be asked. Then, design your tools that allow the agent to query exactly that data for that
use case.
A good reference for basic tools that an observability MCP server provides is by looking at the
top vendors in the observability space and seeing what they provide. Here is a quick sample
overview of the tools idx_6e720362 they are idx_b24b55f6 providing through their MCP servers. For a full list of exported
tools, please check out the documentation of those vendors:

The preceding table is hopefully a good starting point for building your own observability MCP
server. Now, let's walk through some additional best practices and tips.
Tip: Don't mix read and write
The most common use cases for observability MCP servers are providing tools around data
access, such as get_logs, list_spans, list_problems, or execute_query. Those are all read-
access tools, meaning you are querying data from the observability tool. Another set of use
cases is around configuration or triggering actions on the observability tool, such as
create_workflow_for_notification, send_notification, or setup_slo.
The best practice is not to mix data access with other operations into a single MCP server. It's
better to provide multiple MCP servers, each targeted for its specific purpose. The reasons for
this guidance are as follows:
It avoids accidental execution of operations that modify observability configuration or
that trigger automation.
It reduces the attack surface when hackers try to do prompt injections. To read more
about this, check out the documentation on this from Invariant Labs [5].
•
•
207 The Observability Agent: Real-Life Use Cases
While it's possible for a user of an MCP server to select which tools should be active and which
ones not, it turns out that the majority just go with the default and always enable all tools.
To sum it up, if you intend to provide read and write access to your observability platform, it's a
good practice to separate those tools into separate MCP servers that must be installed
separately. You could call them Observability MCP Data Access and Observability MCP
Admin, as most write-access idx_62153e3f operations idx_1eadb22a are typically administrative!
Tip: Generic versus use case-specific
Most observability backends provide an API to execute generic queries with the query language
of the platform, such as with NRQL (New Relic), DDSQL (DataDog), DQL (Dynatrace), or
PromQL (Prometheus). For read access, it would therefore be sufficient to just offer a generic
execute_query tool, and then the agentic AI can use that tool to query any type of data that is
needed. While such a method is definitely needed, it is advisable to also think about more

chunks.title: observabilityintheai-nativeera
chunks.heading: Chapter 6 206
chunks.content:
specific tools that return a specific set of data that is often requested, for example, get_logs,
list_incidents, or fetch_spans. While capturing logs can also be done through
execute_query, the get_logs tool can provide additional parameters for specific filtering on
logs, such as timespan, workload identifier, or hostname. get_logs can then craft the right
optimized query to retrieve exactly that requested data. This eliminates the need for the
agentic AI to guess the correct query in the target query language to achieve the same result.
The problem here lies in the word guess because, very often, an agentic AI doesn't come up with
the best optimized query from the start. Based on experience, those agents start with a broader
query or even queries that are not correct initially. They retry by refining the query until they
get the desired result. That refinement process not only takes time, but it also consumes
resources and often incurs additional costs, as every query API call to the backend observability
system typically comes with some type of query cost.
On the other end of the spectrum, it doesn't make sense to provide a tool for every specific use
case. For instance, it's not advisable to provide separate tools such as get_logs_from_k8s,
get_logs_from_hosts, get_logs_from_apps, and get_logs_from_serverless. While it's
possible to go that fine-grained, you need to consider whether this is really helpful, as you need
to maintain a lot of tool implementations, and there is a chance that the agent chooses the
wrong tool initially.
To sum it up, think about the questions and the top use cases your MCP server will serve. If a
common use case is to identify patterns in logs, then maybe provide a tool that is called
analyze_logs. This can execute the optimized queries to detect problematic log patterns and
return the result in a single call. This avoids a situation where an agent must execute many
different execute_query calls and then do the pattern identification based on all the data
returned. If it's more efficient to do all this within the observability platform, then do it there.

Tip: Local versus remote validation
When an agent is prompted with Give me an overview of all critical logs from yesterday, the agent
tries to craft a query based on the target observability platform's query language. What we
have observed is that the initial query that gets passed to the execute_query tool is often not
fully valid. We see a lot of syntax errors, as things such as yesterday might be represented in
different ways depending on the query language. The agent will overcome this problem by
updating the query based on any failure that comes back from the MCP server in a trial-and-
error fashion. And while, in the end, we get a valid result, it means that multiple round-trips to
the backend observability platform were necessary.
One way to optimize those round-trips is to add local validations into your MCP server that do
some basic checks, such as whether the query is syntactically correct, and whether the user has
permissions to access idx_be2671a0 this type of idx_e59a8b36 data. The syntax validation check alone will give the agent
immediate feedback, avoiding the additional round-trip to the backend observability platform.
This is faster, saves a network round-trip, and typically also saves costs on the backend.
Ideally, you have some observability of your MCP server and measure how many tool
executions fail due to incorrect queries or insufficient permissions. This gives you enough
evidence to add some local validation to your MCP server. We will talk more about the
observability of your MCP server in the Tracking and measuring usage and impact section later in
this chapter.
To sum it up, agents will not always get the optimal parameters for your tools on the first
attempt. If you understand the most common reasons why tool executions fail, you can add
local validation instead of leaving it all to the observability backend to validate any input. This
will greatly improve performance and save costs.
Now that we have a good understanding of how to connect our observability platform to
agents via tools idx_5db8835a exposed through an MCP server, let's dive into how to provide additional
guidance on how to use those tools.
Providing guidance: Instruction files for your AI agents
In the introduction of idx_3d55cba9 this section, we talked about idx_bfb422dd providing guidance to the AI agent to
elevate from being an apprentice to becoming a master in observability. Depending on the LLM
you use for your agents, the agent might already have some familiarity with observability and
therefore understands concepts such as logs, metrics, traces, or what a k8s cluster is. But
unless you use self-trained models with expert knowledge on the specific setup of your
observability platform, chances are that your agent really is only on an apprentice level.

domain knowledge to the agent without having to train a full LLM with all the insights. The

Without those instructions, an agent would simply start down an exploratory path of
gathering information. Exploration is a good thing, but it's time- and resource-consuming. If
you are an SRE and need a quick, deterministic answer to specific questions, the instruction file
achieves exactly that goal.
Instructions can become very detailed. The important part of the instructions is that you
specify clearly the situation, the goal, and the approach to take to achieve that goal.
Agents, by default, are only as good as the model you are using. While training your own model
is one option, you should consider using instruction files to give clear guidance on how the
agent should execute certain tasks that are asked through prompts. Make sure to read the
documentation of the agentic AI you are using. Follow the best practices on how to provide
instructions and find ways to distribute those instructions to every engineer who leverages
those agents.
Now that we know how idx_a0afd08a to improve the efficiency of our agents, we need to look into how we
can track the usage, measure performance and accuracy, and use this to optimize impact and
costs.
Optimization tip
To optimize querying and analyzing observability data, give instructions that reflect
good practices that experienced performance engineers would follow. That includes
metrics-first analysis, meaning first try to find answers in metrics as they are faster
and cheaper to query. Also, always specify a timeframe when querying data. The more
specific you make your prompt about the type of data and timeframe to analyze, the
faster and cheaper the executed queries will be. Adding this to your instruction files
ensures that your agentic AI calls your MCP server with these best practices in mind.
Tip

Tracking and measuring usage and impact
Like with any software idx_17e0a17d service, app, or feature, it's important to track its usage, adoption, and
costs. The same goes for an MCP server. When building an MCP server that provides 10
different tools, but only 2 of them are used occasionally, the questions we need to answer are
the following:
Why are 80% of the tools not used? Shall we remove them? Or do we need to increase
the description and instruction files for agents to better leverage them?
Why is adoption low? Are there use cases that are missing? Is the data coming back of
poor quality, does it take too long, or is it too costly?
How can we get better feedback from our users about what they like and what should
be improved?
The solution to this is proper monitoring of your MCP server implementation. We need to use
the same observability best practices that we have discussed throughout this book. We need to
think about which metrics give us the insights about performance, usage, accuracy, or costs of

the MCP server tools executions. We need to think about whether we need to add specific logs
for any troubleshooting or whether we need to look into distributed traces to better
understand the full agentic AI workflow, which also includes calling our MCP server.
Instrumenting the MCP server and beyond
You have many idx_fdffb776 options to instrument your own code. We recommend looking into
OpenTelemetry, which idx_def5540b we have covered extensively throughout Chapter 1 and Chapter 3. On
top of OpenTelemetry, there is the open source framework OpenLLMetry [6] from idx_7164d27e Traceloop.
OpenLLMetry provides OpenTelemetry-based observability for your LLM applications,
including support for MCP. It means you automatically get automated distributed traces, logs,
and metrics for all interactions with your MCP server. And it doesn't stop at your MCP.
OpenLLMetry provides insights when calling LLMs, vector DBs, or agentic frameworks such as
Anthropic, Amazon Bedrock, LangChain, LangGraph, Ollama, or OpenAI.

Chances are that you will be integrating your observability platform into various different
agentic AIs to enable different personas in different tools to make better decisions based on
your observability data. In the next section, called Defining personas: Who is using the AI and
where?, we will talk about all those various use cases. It will become clear that we really need to
understand the end-to-end agentic AI workflow executions in order to understand usage,
adoption, and impact.
You might be using an agent in either of the following:
The IDE to support your engineers in making better coding decisions
The issue tracking system to enrich bug details with live observability data
The support ticket system to provide end user impact analysis
The CRM system to enrich customer information with the issues they ran into
The business reporting system to correlate business KPIs with technical problems
In any scenario where you are using or planning to use off-the-shelf or custom-built agents,
you should implement agentic AI observability. And this is not limited to only the use cases
where you interact with your observability backend, but should expand to all agentic AI use
cases and all the tools it connects to.
The emerging topic of AI observability probably needs a dedicated chapter or even its own
book. There is already plenty of material out there, but we wanted to make sure it also gets a
mention here. Thanks to open standards such as OpenTelemetry and OpenLLMetry, agentic
systems can be observed without too much of an effort. Check out the documentation of your
agentic AI development kit or talk to the vendor of your agentic AI solution to see how you can
get end-to-end workflow observability through OpenTelemetry sent to your observability
backend.

Chapter 6 216
We are just scratching idx_da3d924b the surface here on the topic of agentic AI and LLM observability. Stay
up to date on the latest developments in that space, consult the documentation of the
frameworks and tools you are using, and strive to ingest traces, logs, and metrics into your
observability platform.
In this section, we covered what observability information should be exposed to an agent via
MCP, how to track its usage, and how to provide instructions for agents to elevate from an
apprentice to becoming masters of observability. We learned that agentic AIs are going to help
many different personas in their day-to-day work and that it's important to observe those
agents to identify their usage, internal workings, and costs. In the next section, we will take a
closer look at the idx_07fa1ac3 personas idx_118a544c and the use cases where observability data can help them make
better-informed decisions in the tools and processes they already use.
Defining personas: Who is using the AI and where?
We already got to idx_5a74dc20 know Christian, a software engineer who leverages an agentic AI in his
Visual Studio Code with prompts such as " Are there any problems with my app in production? If
yes, please investigate them, and let me know where in the code I can fix them! "
A lot of the observability-enabled use cases that get discussed at conferences or blogs focus on
how to improve the day-to-day activities of a software engineer in their IDE. But there are
many other people involved in planning, developing, testing, operating, and optimizing
software that can benefit from observability data that gets brought into their day-to-day
processes and used with tools through an AI. In this section, we will explore those use cases so
you can better understand where else observability and AI can have a major efficiency impact.
Who are your internal end users and their use cases?
If we look at the DevOps idx_25fbb5cc infinity loop that we used in Chapter 3 in the Tracking the SDLC
section, we see a lot of activities between planning, coding, deploying, and operating software.
In each phase, we have different types of engineers needing to make decisions about their next
step. In most of those steps, observability can help to make better-informed decisions. Let's
walk through some examples by looking at prompts that those individuals might want to
execute!
217 The Observability Agent: Real-Life Use Cases
Planning: What features to build, improve, or remove?
I am the product owner of our online customer self-service portal and need to plan our product
roadmap for the next 6 months to guide our engineers on what they need to work on. Analyze the
current feature usage of our online customer banking portal in production and identify the top and
least used features of that portal. Find out how much effort we currently put into maintaining all those

chunks.content:
features by analyzing the existing Jira tickets for those features. Then give recommendations on which
features we should remove without breaking core system functionality, which features we should
improve to increase user interactions, and give a time estimate for all those steps.
Whether done through a human or an AI agent, observability provides critical insights to the
preceding prompt, such as which features are currently used and which ones aren't, what are
critical user journeys that require certain features even though they might not be used often,
and which features have bad performance or high failure rates and therefore impact user
experience and should be optimized?
While we talk about end-user features here, the same prompt would also work for non-end-
user-facing software systems, such as APIs that you are exposing for external consumption.
Clearly, though, this prompt will save any product owner or business analyst a lot of time and
give them insights to make better decisions in their day-to-day work.
Building: How to improve the resiliency of our architecture
I am a software architect and am responsible for the cloud-native architecture of our core banking
system. Some of the services come from a vendor, but most of our services are custom-developed. All
workloads are properly tagged to distinguish them. Analyze all the problems we had in our own
software components over the past 6 months. Give me an analysis of problem areas, root causes, and
their impact on our end users. Provide suggestions on what improvements we can make to our code,
deployments, usage of existing cloud services, and architecture to reduce the risk of running into those
same problems again.
Software architects typically analyze their deployments and the dependencies between the
deployed services. They look at metrics to understand load behavior and extract dependency
information from distributed traces to understand cross-service impact. When tagging is done
properly, then all tag information is also available in the observability platform, as discussed in

While the final decision is still in the hands of the architects, getting an answer to this prompt
from an agent that analyzes the rich data in the observability platform via an MCP allows them

I am leading the quality engineering team, and my goal is to increase test coverage of our critical
backend APIs. I want to start by focusing on APIs that currently have no tests, and then move on to APIs
that do have tests but have still caused issues in production over the past year. Let's start with the
transfer-fund service. Identify the top 10 API calls of that service and give a recommendation on which

Use case – FinOps: redistributing workloads
FinOps is a critical topic idx_8857fb05 for all organizations as it aims to optimize resource utilization to meet
both business needs while staying within financial boundaries.
FinOps teams, therefore, constantly analyze the demand for specific services or workloads and
how those demands change. If a certain service or application is now used by more users than
before, it may need an upgrade. It could also be the other way around: a service is less used
than in the past and can now run with a fraction of the initially allotted resources.
Observability can be used to identify the actual requirements of resources of a workload over
time. FinOps teams analyze historical data or use algorithms to predict future resource
utilization by considering changes in the usage behavior of upstream services. This data can
then be used to distribute those workloads to the right shared infrastructure.
Another use case relates to hardware, especially from cloud vendors, which is constantly
updated with new chipsets. Observability can tell you which workloads are GPU-intensive, and
you can use that information to move them to hardware that is optimized for those types of
workloads if performance is a key requirement.

importantly, the company's reputation was being negatively impacted, and that was making it

The task force had a huge job in front of them and started by digging into the root causes of the

The cost drivers
The observability working idx_9c127dff group started work on determining why the operations spend did
not decrease as they expected. The working group knew they needed data in order to focus on
the area(s) driving the largest expenditures. Since all of the changes were kept on-premises
and all deployed resources were labeled well, it was a rather simple process to gather the cost
data on the new infrastructure deployed as part of the observability improvements.
After gathering and analyzing the costs for the new infrastructure, the working group realized
that the costs for the new observability tooling were much higher than they had expected.
More compute resources were required than planned, which meant that not only were the
licensing expenses higher than expected, but the infrastructure costs to run the tool were
higher as well.
The working group also decided to do some research about costs related to observability and AI
projects. What they found surprised and dismayed them because they discovered that many AI
projects fail. They found that a McKinsey report showed only one-third of all AI projects make
it into production (https://www.mckinsey.com/capabilities/quantumblack/our-
insights/the-state-of-ai), which means two-thirds of AI projects are failing or stalling.
While they didn't find a single reason why those projects fail, they did find a few problems that
can cause AI projects to fail. AI needs good data in order to provide any utility. Despite the
training and work the team had put into the effort, they didn't have a clear idea of whether the
data the company was producing was of good enough quality. They thought it was possible
their data was just good enough to provide some utility while also causing a lot of wasted time,
and that could also be a cost driver.
The observability working group also realized that they would need to determine a way to
track cost savings for this initiative so they could present the benefits to senior leadership.
While they had some avenues to pursue to improve costs, it was becoming obvious that the
cost savings might not show up in the cost of operations alone. Results such as reducing
downtime, preventing outages, and even improving application development team design are
all benefits with real financial impacts that would be missed by looking at the operational cost
alone.
As a starting point, the working group decided they needed to talk with the users of the
observability tools in order to understand how the observability tools are being used and the
value they are providing. This meant getting input from the SREs and application development
teams to assess idx_ef606c1d whether the tooling helped them. Without good data, even the best SREs or
developers will struggle, and if the tooling isn't providing those groups with useful

A new challenge: Business process observability
A funny thing idx_9e82b1ae happened as the observability working group was gearing up to dive into the
soaring costs of their observability journey. Business leaders reached out to the working group
with a problem they hoped the observability improvements could address.
ACME Financial Services is a large and complex company that serves many different markets

The observability working group hadn't considered this aspect of the work they had been

The observability tooling itself wasn't easy to navigate for people not familiar with

How observability can help with compliance
Since ACME idx_2d43bf8e Financial Services provides services in many highly regulated industries in
multiple countries, they are subject to a lot of regulations, and they must ensure that they are
compliant with those regulations. Many times, decisions may be more conservative than
necessary just to ensure there is no threat of a regulation violation. Up until this point,
regulation compliance at ACME Financial Services has largely been ensured via rigorous
controls and planning processes. While not perfect, the results have largely kept ACME
Financial Services out of trouble with the various regulators. However, nothing is free, and the
cost for the current process is a reduction in development and deployment speed.
Once the observability working group recognized the opportunity from widening the
definition of observability, they started to look at what else they could impact and improve
across the company. Along the same vein as cluster scaling, the working group realized that if

events, and so on, they could use ACME Observability to monitor and report on compliance

were the same frameworks that ACME Financial Services was required to meet.
This revelation felt like a game-changer to the working group. Instead of having to rely upon
rigid and slow processes, they could have real-time data and visualization of that data,
showing how compliant resources were with various regulations. They wouldn't have to slow
innovation and hope for compliance; instead, they would be able to tell whether a change
weakened or strengthened their compliance with regulations. It would also provide a roadmap

Tackling the costs
Up to this point, the idx_46161fa7 observability working group hadn't really done very much investigation
into actually reducing costs. They had discovered many new ways that ACME Observability
could be used to improve productivity, but they didn't have a very good understanding of how
much that might increase their cost. With senior leadership very unhappy with the operation
costs for the business, the working group knew they needed to find some ways to reduce costs,
or at the very least, provide strong justifications for those costs since they had originally
pitched a reduction in cost.
The working group decided they should start by discussing their cost concerns with the ACME
Observability vendor. In that discussion, the observability working group detailed how they
were using the tool and how it was deployed. They highlighted that every application team
was sending every piece of telemetry data to the tool every time their applications performed
any work. They felt that this would ensure that all the data needed to assess production
incidents would be available in the tool. They likened this approach to how they provided
production logs to their log aggregator.
After listening to ACME Financial Services detail their tool usage and problems, the ACME
Observability vendor highlighted a big concern with how the tool is being used. They pointed
out that ACME Financial Services is a large company with many applications running that
produce a lot of telemetry data. Processing and storing all of that data would be very expensive,
and they returned to the analogy used by the ACME Financial Services team when they

detailed how they used their log aggregator. Because applications generally produce a lot of log

data, ACME Financial Services has a policy that debug logging should be disabled when
applications are deployed to production. The ACME Observability vendor equated that policy
with a similar policy in the observability world idx_b5eb6d42 called sampling. In large companies such as
ACME Financial Services, it is not viable to process and store every piece of telemetry data if a
desired goal is to be financially responsible. That is why ACME Observability, and the industry
at large, recommends using sampling to reduce that storage and processing burden while still
maintaining all the data necessary to identify the root cause of incidents. The ACME
Observability vendor recommended investigating and implementing sampling strategies to
reduce the cost of running their tooling.
Assessing sampling
After their meeting with ACME Observability, the working group realized they had more
research to do around sampling. According to the vendor, sampling could provide significant
cost savings, but they didn't really understand how to implement it in a single application, let
alone across the entire company.
The working group researched sampling and discovered that while it is a common practice for
dealing with large amounts of telemetry data, there isn't a single, or even simple,
implementation of sampling. There are a few common strategies, such as head, tail, or random
sampling, but which strategy is best can depend on what is important for diagnosing
production issues.
The group decided to idx_60c03052 use a simple example as an exercise to understand how sampling would
help control costs. They decided on using the maximum number of connections per hour,
which could be an indicator to help scale an application. The group decided to try evaluating
two data sampling methods: head sampling and tail sampling.
Head sampling makes a decision about the metric data at the beginning of an interval, and tail
sampling makes a decision about the data after you have all the metrics for the time interval.
Their idea was that an application would only need to report the metric if the number of
connections being managed had increased when the connection was initiated. It was a simple
configuration, but at some point, the application would need to reset its internal counter to
ensure proper reporting over an hour timeframe. In their evaluation of this scenario, they
determined that latency and connection errors would probably be lost. Any sharp spikes or
drops in connections over the course of that hour would also not be accurately identified. The
group wasn't sure whether that was an acceptable trade-off for all applications. In fact, for

chunks.heading: Chapter 7 246

anything time-sensitive, such as a trading application, those trade-offs probably would not be
acceptable.
The group then decided to evaluate that same example using tail sampling. In this scenario,
they determined that errors and latency issues would be surfaced, but each application in the

connection flow would likely need more CPU and memory in order to manage the trace data.
Having all the data would make it easier to identify spikes, but that would be an additional
calculation, and it's hard to know whether a spike is important or just expected based on
system design. Are these trade-offs acceptable? Is the cost of increased memory and CPU less
than the storage cost savings gained by using tail sampling? Is there enough cost offset gained
by removing the need for storing larger data blocks about connection information long-term?
The group wasn't confident they could answer that question without assistance from an

It is also possible that technologies change the implementation or even the sampling strategy.

As complicated as sampling appeared to be, it also appeared to be the only real solution to their
cost problem. The observability working group didn't think they should even attempt to decide

idx_1e0b0f9b materials for the application teams to consume and implement. They didn't see a better way,

A platform team?
The observability working group discovered that their problem was not unique and, in fact,
was pretty common in these kinds of changes in large organizations. It is very hard to
coordinate application development teams around a set of documented standards. The more
complex the situation, the less defined the standard can be, and that leads to differences in
implementation. The solution to their problem is not just using their tooling better, but also
building their software in a repeatable, standardized way.
One of the proposed solutions to such a problem is a centralized team that provides a common
implementation of important standards and the mechanism for building and deploying
software that meets those standards. This has the benefit of putting all of the implementation
work in one team, and the results of their work are consumed by all the application teams. The
application teams don't have to worry about interpreting complex standards, and that reduces
or even eliminates the implementation differences for those core standards. In observability, it
is still important to allow application teams to provide data unique to their application, but
there is a lot of data that can be defined in a common way by a common team. The
observability working group discovered that a centralized team that performs this type of work
is often referred to idx_5b3ea627 as a platform team, and their method for doing so was through the creation
idx_8db24113 of an internal developer platform (IDP).
A big ask, a big undertaking
The observability idx_c1f9bd60 working group decided that the company would need a platform team to
design and implement common standards and to help drive application teams toward
standards-compliant implementations in their applications for their unique use cases. They
also realized that this was much easier said than done. It was one thing to create training and
rely on the application development teams to do the work, and quite another to have a
centralized team, or teams, performing that work. The latter would probably require some kind
of company reorganization and possibly some shift in responsibilities at the management
level. That is a big ask of senior leadership, and they knew that they could not make such a
request without clearly defining the work and responsibilities of that team.

SREs were responsible for keeping the applications running, and that included handling
outages and scaling application resources as needed. Since the application teams had a base

changes they made to the application deployment to the application teams to ensure that the
deployment configuration was updated and production changes weren't rolled back on a new

Reactive versus proactive scaling
The first topic idx_dd4c7cc7 the observability working group wanted to discuss idx_58d390ce was using observability data
to scale the Kubernetes clusters. The working group members didn't really understand how,
but they knew that the Kubernetes clusters were scaling and able to handle increased loads, so
they didn't understand how using observability data would help anything. They didn't want to
highlight this in their presentation to senior leadership if they couldn't talk to and defend the
proposed improvement.
The SREs started by explaining how the Kubernetes clusters were currently scaled. They were
generally scaled in one of two ways:
Using a Kubernetes tool called idx_b4b07a00 the Cluster Autoscaler (CAS)
Using a time-based action to increase or decrease the size of the Kubernetes cluster
The SREs explained that CAS would increase the size of a Kubernetes cluster when a Pod was
unable to be scheduled on the cluster, and scale down the cluster when it determined that
nodes were being underutilized. There are other tools that could replace CAS, such as
Karpenter or a cloud provider scaling solution, but they generally work the same way. They
scale the Kubernetes cluster only once a need is detected.
The time-based actions to scale a cluster are used when the SREs know the company will
experience an increase in traffic and therefore need more cluster resources. They explained that
this is a brute-force way to try to handle periods of time with known increased traffic. They
used trading markets as an example. Trading markets are only open during a period of time
during the day, but at night, the demand on trading systems is much lower. To account for this
in a cost effective manner, the SREs have put in place time based actions to scale up the cluster
before the trading markets open to be able to handle the surge of traffic that usually occurs at
that time, and then at the end of the trading day, they will scale down the cluster to reduce
costs since traffic drops off significantly during the evening.
The SREs then explained that the two methods they just highlighted are reactive, meaning they
can only act when defined limits are reached. Scaling a Kubernetes cluster is not
instantaneous, so even with the CAS, there is still a period of time where the system is under
stress until the new Kubernetes nodes are spun up and added to the cluster. The time-based
actions are really a poor attempt at being proactive. Through years of experience providing
services and managing traffic loads, the SREs had learned when there tends to be increased
demand within the company's offerings and had automated scaling of the Kubernetes clusters
accordingly.
While those current techniques work, they still leave a lot of room for improvement. For

Automating regulation compliance
Another feature of idx_d05955f2 ACME Observability that wasn't being used was regulation compliance.
The SREs explained that ACME Observability supported reporting compliance with various
regulations. This work was currently handled in a rather manual fashion by a regulation
compliance department. The process tended to require application teams to engage with the
compliance department when they thought a change might run afoul of a regulation. This was
less than foolproof because the application development teams didn't know the details of any
regulations. In general, there were some processes in place to help elevate architecture and
especially security design decisions to a group of senior decision makers, and that group
usually had enough knowledge to know if compliance needed to be consulted.
ACME Observability could automate compliance and help reduce the possibility of changes
that would violate a regulation from being deployed into production. Since the tool supported
reporting the level of compliance with various regulations, that data could also be queried by

Expanding left: Meeting developers where they work
The observability working idx_1d83d02d group had spent a lot of time talking to SREs and understanding
how they could improve their lives and various processes the application development teams
had to undertake. However, they still needed to solve the other half of their problem with the
observability tooling, which was that the application development teams weren't really using
it. The interface was too confusing for them, and they had a difficult time making sense of the
data, so the result was that the application developers didn't really use the tools. The working
group realized that they needed to maximize the return on the tooling to help mitigate senior
leadership's concerns over the costs.
When the observability working group evaluated tools, many of them mentioned supporting
expanding left for observability data. They dove back into ACME Observability's feature set
and documentation and looked for how it could better support the application developers.
They discovered that there were a number of ways the tool could help application developers,
and they would be enabled when more systems were connected to ACME Observability. This
was a fortuitous discovery because it fit into the work already planned in the proposal.
They also learned that it is not uncommon for application developers to shy away from
observability tooling. The tools generally are not designed in a way that integrates well with an
application developer's workflow, and because of that, they tend to be underutilized. Because
this is a common issue, there are integrations and features that can help address the problem.

Observability-driven development
The observability idx_ddabedd1 working group also stumbled across the concept of observability-driven
development. This approach is part of the expanding left effort and works to improve the data
consumed by the observability tools and, therefore, improve the ability to monitor an
application. As the working group noted early in this effort, the better the data, the better the
results.
The application developers would likely see benefits just from tying various development and
observability systems together, but the effect would be amplified if the application developers
considered how to observe the internal state and actions of their applications. This is where
observability-driven development would come into play.
The working group learned that if application developers consider how to design their
applications to support being observed externally, that mentality often leads to application
designs that make it easier for the application developers to diagnose problems. In effect, the
application development teams end up helping themselves in addition to the operations
teams. It also helps application developers continually improve their applications when their
tools receive observability data, which, in turn, improves company response times as a whole.
Unlike just plugging ACME Observability into tools used by application developers, this effort
would require significant training and some changes to the application development process.
Like other development processes, incorporating observability-driven development into an
application's development cycle would require some changes to how applications are designed
and how developers test those applications. It would need to be a central part of the process
and not an afterthought. The observability working group knew they could create training, but

Bringing it all together: The new proposal to senior
leadership
The observability idx_c6350875 working group finally completed its latest investigations into how to
improve observability within ACME Financial Services. What started primarily as a quest to
reduce costs grew into a much wider and more complicated proposal than the one they put
together several years ago. The group had learned that what constituted good observability
practices had changed much more than they originally thought, but that the benefits were also
much larger than they originally thought.
The working group was a little nervous about presenting the proposal to senior leadership. The
last proposal was fairly straightforward and didn't involve a whole lot of major changes within
the company. While it provided significant improvements, it did not come cheaply. Trying to
address the cost of the solution led them to discover their work was far from over. The working
group created a proposal for senior leadership that covered not just cost-cutting, but also
demonstrating the value of the tooling across the software development lifecycle as a means to
justify the investment.
It was a complex proposal with several suggestions addressing more than one area. It would
require some level of reorganization of personnel and responsibilities, as well as company-
wide policy changes, in order to achieve all the benefits they laid out. It also relied upon some
direct and indirect methods to lower costs by taking a look at the entire operations expense
rather than just the direct cost of the tooling. In order to support this approach, they also
highlighted new metrics that would be collected to track how the changes impacted various
parts of the company. The working group knew these metrics could make or break the success
of the project, because without them, it became almost impossible to assess the impact of the
work being done by the observability tooling or the platform team in financial terms.
In addition to the metrics, the working group knew they would need to get senior leadership to
expand their view on costs and savings. With the proposal integrating and affecting many
more parts of the company, the operations cost could no longer be looked at in isolation to
understand the full impact or cost savings of the proposal. This was critically important since
one of the requests from senior leadership that started the first investigation, and was more
central in the second, was around lowering operations costs.

adjust to evaluating and requesting recommendations from the observability tooling as part of

In addition to the company reorganization, metrics, and cost reductions, the observability

were confident that gaining insight into all the actions for a business task would provide
immense benefit. They were confident that senior leadership would like that part of the
proposal, but they knew they needed to emphasize that it would be incredibly difficult to
achieve without the standards and common practices that would be provided by the platform
team.
The plan relied not just on the structural changes, but also on senior leadership commitment.
It would be incredibly difficult to enact the necessary changes across the company without
senior leadership pushing and supporting the efforts. This, along with the reorganization
needed for the creation of the platform team, was the biggest concern the observability
working group had as they prepared to present their plan to senior leadership.
